Hacknet is deceptively simple.  I never thought I'd enjoy a game like this, but this experience was so far beyond my expectations that I cannot properly convey how well-made it is.  The story is quality over quantity, the gameplay is literally just typing commands and clicking and reading, but I couldn't put this game down until I finished it and its DLC in one big-ass 8 hour session.

There is one single sequence that is an absolute masterclass in "do more with less," the final connection of the main storyline.  Without spoiling anything, I want you - yes, you, the person reading this now - to buy Hacknet and put in headphones and experience that sequence for yourself.  If Hacknet is on sale, it's an absolute must buy.  Buy a few copies for your friends.  Support this dev.  Hack the planet.

I thought I reviewed this but apparently not.  This game or more specifically the old alpha build back in 2012 is what got me hooked on hacking sims.  Especially ones with parser setups where you manually write out the commands in the terminal.  This version is bigger and wider and avoiding spoilers the "grand finale" is pretty crazy.  The Labyrinth DLC expands it with a lot more extra stuff to do and find.  And the mods... while a game shouldn't rely on mods for more content the mods here craft anything from small quick quests to full on hacking campaigns with unique twists on the gameplay.

I highly recommend playing this game if you're looking for a hacking sim.  Whether on sale or not - although it has gone as low as $3 for the full game which is a steal - it is fun and frustrating but one of the best hacking sims out there.  If admittedly fairly simple compared to other hacking sims but that's both a pro and con in itself.

I can't remember for certain but it's likely that I came across Hacknet from reviews after I played Uplink which I really enjoyed. Since Hacket was equally as low priced I bought it and finally got around to playing it. Initially I struggled, because even though Uplink's GUI is dated, at least it has one, and it took a while for me to get used to hacknet's mostly typing style. I enjoyed the story unfolding, but it soon felt similar to Uplink in that the hacking process started to feel repetitive and somewhat boring. Uplink had the mechanism to improve the hacking machine whereas in Hacknet it is just a case of getting new tools as the story progresses. Uplink had a higher risk and consequence of getting caught - I only finished the story on my 3rd attempt. But in Hacknet the risk and consequences are low but also mostly part of the story. I found that getting traced was sometimes the best way to progress in the parts where the only alternative was to type quicker than I can. Hacknet took me 10 hours to complete, a quarter of what it took me to complete Uplink, so cost per hour is higher, but already very low so that's not a big deal. Whilst I recommend Hacknet, I recommend Uplink more.

With Uplink and Hacknet completed I think I have had my fill of hacking games. The Labyrinth DLC is low cost and the reviews suggest it is good enough to be considered Hacknet 2 on its own. However I don't think I'll get it now that the novelty of such games has gone for me.

I'd only recommend this game if: you get it for free or really cheap, you want a short game to play but don't care what, or you just really want to see lots of scrolling lines and feel like a faux hacker

Otherwise, I don't think it's worth your time for the following reasons:

1. too simple and repetitive
Once you figure out the command lines after a few minutes that's the entire game play. In fact, you'll have to type the same things over so many times you'll mostly use the GUI menu instead. Then, you just wait around all the time waiting for the same 4-5 port hacks to finish that's nothing more than progress bars and flashing numbers like you see in movies. You do this again and again over the next few hours doing simple contracts you pick up from the hacker group postings board (which don't require any thinking since they tell you exactly where to go and what to do which is most of the time just deleting some files off the target server). 

2. lack of story and immersion
As mentioned above, 90% of the time you are doing these simple job postings. The other 10% is the actual story but other than a quick introduction to the missing dead hacker in the beginning, all of its related missions are shoehorned at the end in like the last three missions. Also, another problem I had was the immersion. If you read the files in the folders they want you to target, they're related to the back story of the mission you're doing but if you poke around in the home folder they're just a bunch of random files. For example, it doesn't make sense to read irc chat logs of teenagers making dumb pun jokes and a grocery list in an enterprise server.

3. some poor ui choices
Every IP address you visit is pinned on a board as a node that you can revisit at anytime. However, the nodes become very cluttered towards the end of the game, and critical story nodes at the end are overlapped with a bunch of nodes you visited at the start of the game. I got stuck for a bit for one mission because when I scanned for connected networks I could not see the one out of the five that newly showed up which I needed to go to. It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times.

4. feature bypass/abuse
There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.
